I used to pole vault in high school. I did it more out of hobby and fascination. I was never very competitive and, frankly, never any good at it but my parents wanted me to do some sport and after taking my 3rd or 4th baseball to the face I decided pole vaulting looked cool.

Anyway, just wanted to point out the play-by-play of what is involved in pole vaulting and its most scary-as-fuck moment. You run as fast as you can holding as far back as you can on the pole (the braver you are, the farther back you hold). Full on sprint, you jam the end of the pole into the trough (or bucket) to plant the pole and then you use your shoulders and arms to pull the pole down and towards you to bend the fuck out of it as hard as you can.

Now, here's the scary part. You sit down, or try to as much as you can to plant your ass on the ground. At this point all of your faith is in the pole and in the people who maintain your pole and the safety mats all around you. You are going to use all that kinetic energy from running, from your muscles pulling the pole, and from your ass getting pulled by gravity and your going to transfer it ALL into that flexy fibreglass pole and your going to bend the major fuck out of that pole so it launches you into the sky.

If it works, it's an incredible feeling and hard to explain in words. The feeling of being launched upwards, followed by this zero-G experience, it's just a total rush.

Now, why is this scary? Because poles break, and when they break it is horrifying. I witnessed this a couple of times. You'll see your team mate at the top of his way up only to hear BANG! like a gunshot and the pole exploding and splintering into a zillion pieces. There is a massive amount of energy released when a pole breaks. Depending on when it breaks, you will fall straight down onto your back and neck, but you hope that there'll be enough forward momentum to make it so you sail onto the mats. The force of the shattering pole rings through your wrists and arms. Then, you hope the volunteers set the mats up right and you don't fall through mats that weren't fastened together properly.

I witnessed one guy, the best we have, snap a pole trying for 4.5m jump and he went straight down and broke his neck. Thankfully he did recover after wearing a neck brace for a long time.

Remember I mentioned about putting total faith in the equipment and people in charge of the mats and such? When you start out in pole vaulting, you'll be using loaner equipment, the gym will have a bunch of poles that have been used a million times. They wear out. Also, poles are rated for weight, you want to use the lightest pole you can get away with for your weight - putting more strain on an old pole.

Ultimately, it's a fun sport but it's not for (me) or for the feint of heart!
